meta.description: Not Vonnegut’s own wit: an anonymous graffito joke documented in 1968, years before Vonnegut reprinted a version in Deadeye Dick (1982).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To be is to do. To do is to be. Do be do be do'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous, communally-built graffito joke traced to 1968 — Vonnegut merely reprinted a version in Deadeye Dick (1982), crediting Socrates, Sartre & Sinatra himself.

answer.label: Not Vonnegut’s own line — an anonymous graffito joke
answer.sourceLine: Kurt Vonnegut did print a version — “‘To be is to do’—Socrates. ‘To do is to be’—Jean-Paul Sartre. ‘Do be do be do’—Frank Sinatra” — in his 1982 novel Deadeye Dick, but as graffiti scrawled on a wall, crediting each line to others. He did not originate it: Quote Investigator traces the joke to an anonymous, incrementally-built graffito reported in the Dallas Morning News in January 1968, years before the book. Crediting the wisdom to Vonnegut himself is a misattribution.

source.excerpt: “To be is to do”—Socrates. “To do is to be”—Jean-Paul Sartre. “Do be do be do”—Frank Sinatra.
trail: The anchor investigation: Quote Investigator traces the joke to an anonymous graffito reported by columnist Paul Crume in the Dallas Morning News in January 1968, built up incrementally by three different people on a warehouse wall in Richardson, Texas.

The names are interchangeable filler: over the decades the template swapped in Lao-tzu, Dale Carnegie, Kant, Hegel, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Sartre and Camus — the “Sinatra” punchline (from his 1966 “Strangers in the Night”) usually survives, per Quote Investigator.
Vonnegut’s connection is real but secondary: he reprinted the joke as wall graffiti in Deadeye Dick (1982), which is why it is now widely credited to him, as seen on Goodreads.
source.excerptNote: The form Vonnegut printed in Deadeye Dick (1982) — note he attributes each line to someone else, not himself. The 1968 original ran differently: “The way to do is to be”—Lao-tzu; “The way to be is to do”—Dale Carnegie; “Do be, do be, do”—Frank Sinatra.

source.rightsNote: The wording is anonymous folk humor with no identifiable author: an incrementally-built graffito documented from January 1968. Vonnegut printed one version in Deadeye Dick (1982, in copyright, Delacorte Press / the Vonnegut estate), but as found graffiti he attributed to others — so no single copyrightable authorship attaches to the bare line, and we assert no public-domain status.

author.name: Kurt Vonnegut
author.heading: About Kurt Vonnegut
author.bio: Kurt Vonnegut Jr. (1922–2007) was an American writer famed for darkly comic, humane novels including Slaughterhouse-Five and Cat’s Cradle. In his 1982 novel Deadeye Dick he quoted the “to be is to do” joke as graffiti scrawled on a wall, crediting Socrates, Sartre and Sinatra — not himself. Because his name is a magnet for clever, quotable lines, the internet has since promoted him from the person who copied down the joke to the person who supposedly coined it.

misattribution.heading: How Vonnegut got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic magnet-name capture: a piece of anonymous folk humor drifts onto a famous author because he once wrote it down.

items.why: Vonnegut printed “‘To be is to do’—Socrates… ‘Do be do be do’—Frank Sinatra” in Deadeye Dick (1982) — but as graffiti, crediting others. Quote Investigator shows the joke predates the book by at least 14 years.

items.who: Socrates, Sartre, Kant, Hegel, Lao-tzu, Dale Carnegie
items.why: The philosopher names were never real quotations; they rotate freely across versions of the graffito, per Quote Investigator. Only the Sinatra scat has a genuine source — his 1966 recording of “Strangers in the Night.”

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is an anonymous, incrementally-authored graffito in the Dallas Morning News, January 1968 — nobody, Vonnegut included, coined it as wisdom, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it sticks
lead: The joke works because it collapses centuries of philosophy about essence versus action into a punchline — and then deflates the whole thing with Sinatra’s nonsense scat. It reads like something a witty novelist would write, which is exactly why it keeps getting reassigned to one.
context.pull: Vonnegut copied the joke down. The internet promoted him to its author.
